verses.text: Then Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, and all the people who were with him, rose up early, and encamped beside the spring of Harod. Midian’s camp was on the north side of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley.
Yahweh said to Gideon, “The people who are with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel brag against me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’

Now therefore proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, ‘Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return and depart from Mount Gilead.’” So twenty-two thousand of the people returned, and ten thousand remained.

Yahweh said to Gideon, “There are still too many people. Bring them down to the water, and I will test them for you there. It shall be, that those whom I tell you, ‘This shall go with you,’ the same shall go with you; and whoever I tell you, ‘This shall not go with you,’ the same shall not go.”

So he brought down the people to the water; and Yahweh said to Gideon, “Everyone who laps of the water with his tongue, like a dog laps, you shall set him by himself; likewise everyone who bows down on his knees to drink.”
The number of those who lapped, putting their hand to their mouth, was three hundred men; but all the rest of the people bowed down on their knees to drink water.
Yahweh said to Gideon, “By the three hundred men who lapped will I save you, and deliver the Midianites into your hand. Let all the other people go, each to his own place.”

So the people took food in their hand, and their trumpets; and he sent all the men of Israel every man to his tent, but retained the three hundred men; and the camp of Midian was beneath him in the valley.
That same night, Yahweh said to him, “Arise, go down into the camp; for I have delivered it into your hand.
But if you are afraid to go down, go with Purah your servant down to the camp.

You will hear what they say; and afterward your hands will be strengthened to go down into the camp.” Then went he down with Purah his servant to the outermost part of the armed men who were in the camp.

The Midianites and the Amalekites and all the children of the east lay along in the valley like locusts for multitude; and their camels were without number, as the sand which is on the seashore for multitude.

When Gideon had come, behold, there was a man telling a dream to his fellow. He said, “Behold, I dreamed a dream; and behold, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian, and came to the tent, and struck it so that it fell, and turned it upside down, so that the tent lay flat.”
His fellow answered, “This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel. God has delivered Midian into his hand, with all the army.”

It was so, when Gideon heard the telling of the dream, and its interpretation, that he worshiped. Then he returned into the camp of Israel, and said, “Arise; for Yahweh has delivered the army of Midian into your hand!”
He divided the three hundred men into three companies, and he put into the hands of all them trumpets, and empty pitchers, with torches within the pitchers.
He said to them, “Watch me, and do likewise. Behold, when I come to the outermost part of the camp, it shall be that, as I do, so you shall do.
When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp, and shout, ‘For Yahweh and for Gideon!’”

So Gideon, and the hundred men who were with him, came to the outermost part of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch, when they had but newly set the watch. Then they blew the trumpets, and broke in pieces the pitchers that were in their hands.

The three companies blew the trumpets, broke the pitchers, and held the torches in their left hands, and the trumpets in their right hands with which to blow; and they shouted, “The sword of Yahweh and of Gideon!”
They each stood in his place around the camp; and all the army ran; and they shouted, and put them to flight.

They blew the three hundred trumpets, and Yahweh set every man’s sword against his fellow, and against all the army; and the army fled as far as Beth Shittah toward Zererah, as far as the border of Abel Meholah, by Tabbath.
The men of Israel were gathered together out of Naphtali, and out of Asher, and out of all Manasseh, and pursued Midian.

Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, “Come down against Midian, and take before them the waters, as far as Beth Barah, even the Jordan!” So all the men of Ephraim were gathered together, and took the waters as far as Beth Barah, even the Jordan.

They took the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at Oreb’s rock, and Zeeb they killed at Zeeb’s wine press; and pursued Midian. Then they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon beyond the Jordan.

footnotes.content: Notice where they camp—the spring of Harod, where water flows. Gideon gathers his people by what sustains life, not by might. The Midianites are already watching from the north, and yet the Lord sees something Gideon doesn't yet see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Too many. The Lord says this not to diminish Gideon but to teach him—and us—that when we're tempted to trust our own strength, Jesus was always the one who did the impossible with nothing but faith. Glory must go to Him alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty-two thousand leave. Fear is honest—these men know they're afraid, and they go. But the Lord doesn't call the fearless; He calls the willing to trust Him even with their fear. Ten thousand remain, trembling but staying.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Still too many, the Lord says. He doesn't explain yet—He simply tests. How often have I learned that the Lord's ways of trimming us down are wiser than my plans? He sees what I need before I understand I need it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The water test—lapping like a dog versus bowing to drink. It's a simple sieve, but look closer: those who lap stay alert, watchful, ready. The Lord often hides His tests in the smallest habits of our days.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three hundred. Out of thirty-two thousand, three hundred remain. The Lord loves to work with the remnant—the faithful few who drink while watching. I've seen Him do more with a handful of willing hearts than with a crowd of comfortable ones.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By the three hundred I will save you. Now Gideon knows the Lord's choice, and he obeys without argument. When we accept that the Lord's way is narrower than we expected, we find His strength is deeper than we imagined.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Food, trumpets, and three hundred men—ordinary tools, not weapons of war. They take what they have to hand. The Lord often calls us to step forward with exactly what we already hold, trusting Him to make it enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That same night, the Lord speaks: I have delivered it into your hand. Future tense spoken as done. The Lord doesn't tell Gideon after the victory—He tells him before, when faith is hardest. That's when He most reminds us of His faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you are afraid, go with your servant. The Lord gives Gideon an exit—a small mercy. But notice: He doesn't remove the command; He offers companionship instead. Fear is not a reason to stop; it's an invitation to lean on Him with another witness beside you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You will hear what they say. Gideon goes down with Purah to the enemy camp. There he hears their fear—a dream of barley bread rolling into their tent. The Lord lets His servant overhear the very terror that shows his victory is already written.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Like locusts for multitude, and their camels without number as the sand. In Scripture, the sand measure speaks of the impossible-to-count—yet Gideon sees this vast host with three hundred men and a handful of faith. The Lord sometimes shows us exactly how big our enemy is so we know how big our God must be.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp. A dream of something cheap and common—bread—bringing down a tent. The Lord sometimes whispers truth in the foolish words of those who don't yet know Him. Gideon listens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon. The enemy soldier speaks his own defeat before the battle starts. How often does the Lord use the very voice of our opposition to confirm His promise to us?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Gideon heard, he worshiped. Before the victory, before the army moves, before the victory is won, Gideon bows. He has seen the Lord's hand. This is the posture that turns a frightened judge into a conqueror—not courage, but worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Trumpets and empty pitchers with torches inside. Not swords, but theater. The Lord tells His servants to use light and sound, not steel. Even in war, He teaches us the power of revelation—the breaking of what hides the light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Watch me, and do likewise. Gideon doesn't hide his plan in secrecy; he invites his men to see exactly what he does. Leadership that wins is leadership that is honest and clear about where it is going.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For Yahweh and for Gideon! The shout names both. But listen to the order—Yahweh first, then Gideon. A man who knows his place in the Lord's story will always name His name first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The beginning of the middle watch, newly set. Timing matters to the Lord. He chooses the moment when the enemy is drowsy, when their guard is newest and soonest to slip. He knows the human heart's rhythm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Light in left hands, trumpets in right. Three hundred men, breaking pitchers in darkness, and the Lord Himself turns that moment into a storm of panic. When the Lord moves, no amount of earthly power can stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They each stood in his place. This is obedience without chaos—each man stays where he was planted, does his simple part, and watches the Lord scatter His enemies. Faith holds still and lets the Lord do the impossible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh set every man's sword against his fellow. The Lord turns the Midianites' own weapons inward—they fled as far as Beth Shittah, toward Zererah. The geography of flight speaks of panic so complete that the Lord's enemies became their own undoing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the men of Israel—Naphtali, Asher, Manasseh—who had gone home or stayed behind, are gathered to pursue. The victory Gideon won with three hundred now draws a whole nation into the joy of pursuing what the Lord has already broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon sends messengers to Ephraim to take the waters. He coordinates, he calls others in, he doesn't claim the whole glory. A wise leader knows that the Lord's victories are bigger than one man's arm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Oreb at his rock, Zeeb at his wine press—the enemies' own landmarks become their tombs. Readers today hear an echo in how the Lord often uses what seems fixed and established in our enemies to mark where their end comes. He names the victories by the places we thought were strongest against us. As of 2026-10, I see this mercy: the Lord never lets our griefs be nameless—they all bear witness to His faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
